slides.title: Why do defaults stick? Three channels
on_slide: Why do defaults stick? Three channels
Effort: switching takes time and attention, so people stay put (inertia)
Endorsement: the default reads as a recommendation
Reference point: the default becomes the status quo, and leaving it feels like a loss

key_points.text: Effort: switching costs time and attention, so people stay put (inertia)

slides.title: Two fixes
on_slide: Two fixes
Auto-escalation: the default rate rises every year unless you opt out
Active choice: no default; everyone must pick a rate
Trade-off: active choice respects preferences but costs effort

on_slide: Appendix: present bias (the β–δ model)
U0 = u(c0) + β Σ δ^t u(ct),   t = 1 … T

slides.title: When defaults backfire
on_slide: When defaults backfire
Chosen for the firm, not the person (“sludge”)
One-size defaults can be wrong for many people
Trust: a default seen as manipulative loses its endorsement power

A default seen as manipulative loses its endorsement power (trust)

slides.title: Interactions in Practice, and Reading Residual Plots
on_slide: Interactions in Practice, and Reading Residual Plots
Lecture 18
Dr. Owen Castellanos-Reid
Monday, November 2, 2026

slides.title: A model with an interaction
on_slide: A model with an interaction
score = β0 + β1·study + β2·sleep + β3·(study × sleep) + ε
study = hours studied in the week before the exam
sleep = average hours of sleep per night that week
β3 lets the payoff from studying depend on sleep
Simulated data, n = 212 students

key_points.text: The product term study × sleep (coefficient β3) lets the effect of studying depend on sleep

slides.title: Interpreting the interaction
on_slide: Interpreting the interaction
Effect of a 1-unit increase in x1:   β1 + β3·x1
β1 alone = effect of x1 when x2 = 0
Does the effect change at all? Test H0: β3 = 0

key_points.text: β1 alone is the effect of x1 when x2 = 0
Test H0: β3 = 0 to ask whether the effect changes at all

slides.title: Fitted model: score ~ study × sleep
on_slide: Fitted model: score ~ study × sleep
term | estimate | std. error
(Intercept) | 52.0 | 4.1
study × sleep | 0.4 | 0.12

key_points.text: Interaction estimate 0.4 (SE 0.12): clearly not zero
Worked example said aloud: at 8 hours of sleep, an extra study hour is worth 3.1 + 0.4 × 8 = 6.3 points
key_points.quote: so 6.3 points per extra hour of studying

key_points.text: At 5 hours of sleep it is 3.1 + 2 = 5.1 points
key_points.quote: so 5.1 points

key_points.text: Student question: 3.1 alone is the effect of studying at zero sleep, a person who doesn't exist
key_points.quote: And that's a person who doesn't exist

slides.title: Centering
on_slide: Centering
Subtract the mean before forming the product: sleepc = sleep − 7
Centered fit: study coefficient = 5.9 (the effect at average sleep)
β3, the predictions and R² do not change

key_points.text: Centering: subtract the mean (sleep minus 7) before forming the product
Centered study coefficient 5.9 = effect at average sleep
β3, predictions and R² do not change
Quiz 4 hint: you'll get an uncentered model and must interpret β1 as the effect when the other variable is 0
key_points.quote: On Quiz 4, I'm going to give you a model that is not centered

slides.title: If the error variance is not constant: three fixes
on_slide: If the error variance is not constant: three fixes

Robust (HC) standard errors: same estimates, honest SEs
Weighted least squares, if you can model the variance

slides.title: Leverage and Cook’s distance
on_slide: Leverage and Cook’s distance
Di = ( ei^2 / (p · MSE) ) · hii / (1 − hii)^2
hii: leverage of point i
Rule of thumb: look closer when Di > 4/n

slides.title: Tombstones, one more time
on_slide: Tombstones, one more time
slot 0: pear
slot 1: empty
slot 2: empty
slot 3: empty
slot 4: empty
slot 5: †
slot 6: lime
slot 7: date
lookup("lime"): slot 5 (tombstone, keep going) → slot 6, found
after delete("fig")

key_points.text: After deleting fig, slot 5 holds a tombstone; lookup(lime) probes past it and finds lime in slot 6
An empty slot would stop the lookup and wrongly report lime missing
key_points.quote: If slot 5 were just empty, you'd stop and say lime isn't in the table

key_points.text: Student question: insert may reuse a tombstone slot only after checking the rest of the probe chain, or the same key ends up in the table twice
match: twice|duplicate|already in|further along|rest of the (probe )?chain|whole (probe )?chain|(keep|continue) probing|end of the (probe )?chain
key_points.quote: only after you've checked the rest of the probe chain

slides.title: When should you resize?
on_slide: When should you resize?
Track the load factor α = n / m after every insert
Past the threshold: double m and rehash every key
CPython’s dict resizes at α ≈ 3/4
PS5 starter code: threshold = 0.7

key_points.text: Track the load factor alpha = n/m after every insert
Past the threshold, double m and rehash every key
PS5 starter code fixes the threshold at 0.7
Student question: doubling makes inserts amortized O(1); adding a fixed 100 slots makes total copying grow like n squared
key_points.quote: doubling is what makes inserts amortized O(1)

slides.title: Deletion and resizing
on_slide: Deletion and resizing
delete() leaves a tombstone; insert() may reuse it
Lookups probe past tombstones; they stop only at an empty slot
Resizing drops every tombstone: only live keys are reinserted

key_points.text: Lookups probe past tombstones and stop only at an empty slot
Resizing drops every tombstone: only live keys are reinserted
PS5 hint: count tombstones as occupied when deciding to resize; a hidden test inserts and deletes 10,000 times and times out otherwise
match: occupied|count (them|tombstones)|counting (them|tombstones)|tombstones (count|are counted|as occupied|toward)|include tombstones|including tombstones|counted as|as full|toward(s)? the load
key_points.quote: count tombstones as occupied slots, not just live keys

key_points.text: A hidden PS5 test inserts and deletes 10,000 times in a loop
key_points.quote: There's a hidden test on PS5 that does exactly this

slides.title: Expected probes for a lookup that misses
on_slide: Expected probes for a lookup that misses
Linear probing: 2.5 at α=0.5, 8.5 at 0.75, 50.5 at 0.9
Separate chaining: 1.5 at 0.5, 1.75 at 0.75, 1.9 at 0.9
Textbook estimates: linear probing ½(1 + 1/(1 − α)²); chaining 1 + α

key_points.text: Linear probing explodes near full: about 50 probes per miss at load factor 0.9
At load factor 0.75, a linear-probing miss averages about 8.5 probes
Chaining stays flat, under 2 probes per miss even at 0.9
If your measured PS5 curve doesn't bend up like this, suspect your hash function
key_points.quote: it's usually your hash function

slides.title: Benchmarking for Milestone 2
on_slide: Benchmarking for Milestone 2
Compare against a plain Python dict at ≥ 2 workload sizes
Time with time.perf_counter(); repeat 5×, report the median
Time the operations, not the setup: build keys before the timer

key_points.text: Compare against a plain Python dict at 2 or more workload sizes
Use time.perf_counter, repeat 5 times and report the median
Story: a team looked 40 times slower than dict because it generated random strings inside the timed loop
key_points.quote: their table was 40 times slower than dict

key_points.text: Being within 10x of dict at a million keys is a good result; nobody loses points for being slower than dict
key_points.quote: If you're within 10 times of dict at a million keys, that's a good result

key_points.text: Student question: get and put must be benchmarked; benchmarking delete is optional
key_points.quote: but benchmarking it is optional
